critical_caution: This is nonfiction, not a short story despite its placement in the Collected Stories corpus and its title's echo of genre fiction. Sutin identifies it directly as an essay, written in 1979 and first published in Interzone (1984), later collected in the essay-story anthology I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon. The first-person narrator is Philip K. Dick himself, describing his own apartment building, his own upcoming condominium purchase, and a real neighbor. It is classified here under lane E (Dick's own voice) rather than lane A (fiction), and the 'reading' fields below describe an autobiographical account, not an invented plot.

work.title: Strange Memories of Death
work.later_use: Collected in the essay-story anthology I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon (Doubleday, 1985).

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: Dick describes an October morning in his Orange County apartment building, which has been converted to condominiums; he has decided to buy his unit for $52,000 rather than move, while nearly everyone else has already left. His attention fixes on a reclusive, silent neighbor the building calls the 'Lysol Lady' — a woman no one has ever heard speak, who uses the elevator to avoid other tenants and drenches her apartment in disinfectant against imagined contamination — who is scheduled to be evicted that day because she cannot afford to buy her unit and has, in Dick's view, made herself too functional to qualify for the mental-health advocacy that could block the eviction on grounds of diminished capacity. Reading a newspaper account of a teenage girl who shot up a schoolyard 'because she didn't like Mondays,' Dick develops an extended meditation on the nature of psychosis: that a psychotic person does not take the easy path but perceptually cannot see it, choosing the harder, self-defeating one until 'the impossible closes in' and the person 'freezes' — kinetic death, a term he borrows in spirit from Augustine's observation that there is ultimately 'no place,' only cessation. He reflects that the only thing separating him from the Lysol Lady is money — a social convention as arbitrary, he suggests, as agreeing gold has value or that a tree is third base — and that her refusal to enter society's 'unwritten contract' has doomed her, in his logic, to a kind of self-willed defeat. The essay resolves anticlimactically: when the property manager returns from a trip, Dick learns the Lysol Lady (identified as a Mrs. Archer) was never evicted at all — the Santa Ana Housing Authority found her a subsidized apartment and is paying her rent, a mundane, functioning social safety net succeeding exactly where Dick's dark philosophical spiral had assumed only catastrophe was possible.

structure.form: personal essay in three movements: observation and dread, philosophical digression on psychosis, anticlimactic resolution
movements: Dick's own condominium purchase, his fixation on the Lysol Lady's coming eviction, and his uneasy sense of solidarity with her isolation.
An extended meditation, prompted by a news story about a school shooting, on the nature of psychosis as a perceptual inability to find the easy way out.
The mundane, non-catastrophic resolution: the Lysol Lady was quietly rehoused by a housing authority while Dick was absorbed in imagining her doom.
structure.point_of_view: first person, Dick's own voice throughout, self-implicating and self-questioning rather than observational — he repeatedly measures his own fear of change and his own fragile grip on 'sanity' against hers.
structure.central_device: An essay that builds toward an imagined tragedy through pure philosophical extrapolation and is then deflated by an entirely unremarkable, bureaucratically successful real-world outcome — the meditation on psychosis turns out to have been more about the essayist's own anxieties than about its ostensible subject.

characters.name: Philip K. Dick (narrator)
characters.note: Repeatedly and explicitly identifies his own stability as contingent on money alone — 'money is the official seal of sanity' — refusing to place himself at any secure distance from the woman he is theorizing about.

characters.name: The Lysol Lady (Mrs. Archer)
characters.note: Never given voice or interiority beyond what Dick projects onto her silence; the essay's final paragraph corrects this by revealing she took practical action (Legal Aid, then housing assistance) entirely outside of Dick's imagined narrative for her.

characters.name: Al Newcum
characters.note: The essay's source for the mundane, deflating final fact — that the housing authority had already solved the problem while Dick was composing his psychosis meditation.

settings.name: The Orange County apartment-turned-condominium complex
settings.note: Rendered with the specific, unglamorous detail of a real late-1970s Southern California housing conversion — dead-bolt locks, developer-installed fountains, a hundred-and-twenty-day legal notice period.

motifs: Money as an arbitrary but absolute social convention separating the sane from the psychotic
Silence and facial avoidance as a neighbor's entire visible personality, filled in entirely by the narrator's own projection
Psychosis defined not as taking the easy way out but as a perceptual inability to see that an easy way exists
A philosophical or literary flourish (Augustine's 'we go backward and forward, and there is no place') applied to an ordinary, unheroic social situation
An anticipated catastrophe deflated by an unglamorous, functioning bureaucratic solution the essayist never considered
reading.significance: Sutin frames the piece precisely: Dick, having 'known well the vertigo of losing one's home,' responded to a real, un-fictionalized housing conversion crisis with an essay rather than a story — meaning the philosophical material here (psychosis as a failure of perception, kinetic death, the arbitrariness of sanity's social contract) is offered as Dick's genuine, real-time thinking rather than as material assigned to a character. The essay's real subject may be less the Lysol Lady than Dick's own admitted terror of change and his own fragile claim to normalcy, measured against a woman he never speaks to and knows only by her silence and her smell of disinfectant. Its anticlimactic ending is itself the point: the essay spends most of its length building an elaborate, literary theory of psychotic self-destruction, only to have the real world quietly solve the problem through an ordinary housing authority — undercutting the narrator's own dramatic framework with a fact he had not thought to check.
reading.closing_note: Dick's closing exchange with Al Newcum — 'I wish someone would pay my rent,' answered flatly, 'You're not paying rent, you're buying your apartment' — deflates his own philosophical meditation with a small, exact joke at his own expense.

distinctive_terms.label: Augustine
distinctive_terms.note: Directly quoted: 'Place there is none... We go backward and forward, and there is no place,' used as the essay's philosophical anchor for the concept of kinetic death.

distinctive_terms.label: Fate
distinctive_terms.note: Dick's own phrase — 'my fate is tied to that of the Lysol Lady' — stating the essay's central identification directly.

distinctive_terms.label: Prison
distinctive_terms.note: The building 'formerly looked like a prison' before the developers' renovation — an incidental but telling word choice given the essay's themes of confinement and escape.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: Dick's own explicit, repeated identification of his sanity and stability with the fragile neighbor he is theorizing about, distinguished from her by money alone
an extended philosophical account of psychosis as a perceptual failure to see available options, applied both to a stranger and reflexively to the essayist himself

open_questions: Sutin references Dick's own recurring 'vertigo of losing one's home' — is this documented more fully elsewhere in his biography (an eviction, a foreclosure, a specific move) that this essay is drawing on?

Was Mrs. Archer a real identifiable person, or a composite/pseudonym? The essay's specificity (Legal Aid, Santa Ana Housing Authority, a named sales rep) suggests real events, but this has not been independently verified here.

How does this essay's meditation on psychosis as 'perceptual inability to see the easy way out' relate to Dick's later Exegesis writing on the nature of delusion and reality-testing? Worth a direct comparison once more Exegesis-adjacent material is catalogued.
